code.title: Engine built-ins versus host APIs

followUps:
No. setTimeout is not part of the ECMAScript language; it is a host API that browsers and Node each provide (the HTML standard and Node define it). The engine only knows built-ins like Array and Promise.

You can see it by running a bare engine such as a stand-alone V8 shell: setTimeout is undefined there. That is why the same name behaves slightly differently in Node (it returns a Timeout object) and in a browser (it returns a number).

Firefox uses SpiderMonkey, Safari uses JavaScriptCore, and React Native often runs on Hermes. On the server, Bun runs on JavaScriptCore.

So when someone says "JavaScript runtime" you still need to ask which engine inside it. Speed, supported syntax and debugging tools differ per engine, but the language rules from ECMAScript stay the same. Chrome and Node share V8, so a bug in a V8 built-in shows up in both.

The event loop lives in the host, not in the engine. The engine only runs one piece of code at a time and keeps the call stack; the host decides when the next task, such as a timer callback or a click handler, is handed to it.

In Node the loop is libuv; in browsers it is defined by the HTML standard. One exception worth knowing: promise jobs (microtasks) are defined by ECMAScript itself, but the host chooses when the microtask queue is drained, usually after each task.

code.title: A blocked main thread delays timers

followUps:
It sets how many threads libuv's pool has. The default is 4, and it can be raised up to 1024 by setting the environment variable before the process starts (for example UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 node app.js).

The pool runs file system calls, DNS lookups (dns.lookup), and parts of crypto and zlib. If you start 8 slow fs or pbkdf2 jobs with a pool of 4, the last 4 wait for a free thread. Network sockets do not use the pool, so raising it does not help them.

Measure how late the event loop runs. Use perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() for a histogram, or compare a repeating timer's expected and actual time, as in the sample program. A high p99 delay means something blocks the loop.

const h = require('perf_hooks').monitorEventLoopDelay();
h.enable();
setInterval(() => {
  console.log(h.percentile(99) / 1e6, 'ms');
  h.reset();
}, 5000);

Then take a CPU profile (--cpu-prof) to find the function. A p99 over about 100 ms usually means slow request latency for everyone.

Pick by what you need to share. worker_threads run JS in parallel inside one process and can share memory (SharedArrayBuffer); use them for CPU-heavy tasks. cluster forks several full copies of your server that share one port; use it to use all CPU cores for ordinary request handling. child_process starts any other program (even non-JS), with separate memory and message passing.

Cost order: workers are cheapest to start, processes cost more memory but isolate crashes. Example: resize images in a worker; run 8 cluster processes on 8 cores.

code.title: Web-standard APIs shared by browsers and Node

followUps:
The API is the same, but the environment around it differs. Browser fetch follows CORS, sends cookies according to credentials, and uses the browser cache and the user's proxy. Node's fetch (built on undici) has no CORS check, no cookie jar by default, and no page origin, so relative URLs fail unless you give a full URL.

Both return the same Response with json() and text(), and both reject only on network errors, not on 404 or 500, so check response.ok yourself.

It is a library whose code runs unchanged on the server and in the browser. The word "isomorphic" (or "universal") only describes that portability, not a special technology.

A library stays isomorphic when it uses only built-ins and web-standard APIs, and keeps platform code (file system, DOM) behind small adapters. Example: a date-formatting helper or a validation schema used by both the React form and the API handler, so the rules are written once and cannot drift apart.

code.title: What lands on the global object

followUps:
In an ES module, top-level this is undefined. In a CommonJS file it is module.exports (the same object as exports), because Node wraps the file in a function and calls it with that object as this.

// a.cjs
console.log(this === module.exports); // true
// b.mjs
console.log(this);                    // undefined

So code that writes this.x = 1 at the top level works in CommonJS and throws a TypeError in a module.

Each frame (iframe) is its own realm with its own copy of built-ins, so its Array is a different function from yours. instanceof checks the prototype chain against your realm's Array.prototype, so it returns false.

Use Array.isArray(arr), which works across realms. The same trap applies to Error and Date objects that cross frames or Node's vm contexts, where Object.prototype.toString.call(x) or a brand check is safer.

code.title: Classic script versus module behaviour

followUps:
Use defer for your own app scripts, and async for independent third-party scripts. Both download without blocking HTML parsing. defer scripts run after parsing finishes, in document order, so they can depend on each other and on the DOM. async scripts run as soon as they arrive, in any order.

Example: analytics goes async (it needs nothing); vendor.js then app.js go defer so vendor always runs first. Module scripts are deferred by default.

An import map is a JSON block that tells the browser which URL each bare name means, so import 'lodash' works without a bundler.

<script type="importmap">
{"imports": {"lodash": "/vendor/lodash.js"}}
</script>

Without it, a browser rejects bare specifiers because it has no node_modules to search. The map must appear before the first module script that uses it.

The nomodule attribute makes a script run only in browsers that do NOT understand type="module". Modern browsers ignore that script.

It was used for the "module/nomodule pattern": ship a small modern ES-module build with type="module" and a bigger transpiled bundle with nomodule for old browsers such as Internet Explorer 11. Today it is rarely needed because every current browser supports modules.

code.title: CommonJS copies, ESM live bindings

followUps:
A dual package hazard happens when a package ships both a CJS and an ESM build and an app ends up loading both, so you get two separate copies with separate state.

Example: require('pkg') and import 'pkg' each create their own singleton, so a cache or a class used with instanceof fails across the two copies. Fixes: make the CJS file a thin wrapper that loads the ESM build's state, keep state in one shared CJS file, or publish ESM only (modern Node can require() it).

ESM imports and exports are static: they sit at the top level with fixed names, so a tool can read them without running the code. A bundler can therefore see which exports are never used and drop them ("tree shaking").

CommonJS require is a normal function call and module.exports is an ordinary object that may change at run time (require(name + '.js')), so tools must keep the whole file. Example: importing only { map } from an ESM utility library can remove the other 200 functions from the bundle.

ESM has no __dirname, but import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename exist in Node 20.11 and later. On older versions build them from import.meta.url:

import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { dirname } from 'node:path';
const __filename = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);
const __dirname = dirname(__filename);

import.meta.url is a file:// URL, so it has to be converted to a path.

code.title: Module evaluation order in a cycle

followUps:
Top-level await makes a module's evaluation asynchronous: modules that import it wait until its promise settles before they run, while unrelated sibling modules can keep going.

The graph is still walked depth-first, but a parent runs only after every awaiting dependency finishes. Example: if db.js does await connect() (200 ms), then app.js that imports it starts at about 200 ms. In a cycle, a module cannot wait for one that is already waiting for it, which leads to a hang, so avoid awaiting inside cycles.

CommonJS does not throw a TDZ error; it gives a partly filled object. When b requires a while a is still running, b receives whatever a has put on module.exports so far, which may be an empty object.

// a.js: exports.x = 1 comes AFTER require('./b')
// b.js
const a = require('./a');
console.log(a.x); // undefined, no error

Silent undefined is harder to spot than a ReferenceError. Same fixes: move shared code out, or read a.x lazily inside a function.

code.title: Caret and tilde semver ranges

followUps:
dependencies are needed at run time, devDependencies only to build and test, and peerDependencies say "the host app must supply this package, I will use its copy".

Example: a React component library lists react as a peer, so the app and the library share one React instance (two copies break hooks). Express is a dependency of a server; Jest and ESLint are devDependencies, skipped by npm install --omit=dev in production images.

Pin an exact version (no ^) when a tiny change can break you or when you must be able to reproduce a build exactly: build tools, compilers, code generators, a package with a bad release history, or a security fix you must keep.

Example: pin typescript at 5.4.5 because every minor release can add new type errors. For libraries you publish, avoid pinning dependencies, as that forces duplicate copies on your users; the lockfile already gives exact versions for your own app.

code.title: Node bare-specifier resolution model

followUps:
A phantom dependency is a package your code imports but never declared in package.json; it only works because npm's flat node_modules hoisted it there from another dependency.

When that other package updates, your import breaks. pnpm blocks it: your node_modules holds symlinks only to the packages you declared, and each package's own dependencies live in a separate store folder. Importing an undeclared name then fails right away with "Cannot find module" instead of working by accident.

Both follow the same walk-up-the-folders idea. Bundlers (webpack, Vite) and TypeScript's moduleResolution: "node16" or "nodenext" copy Node's rules, including the exports map and conditions such as import and require.

The older TypeScript "node" mode ignores exports, so a type may resolve to a different file than the real runtime loads. Rule: set moduleResolution to match what actually runs your code, or you can get types that compile but modules that fail at run time.

code.title: Conditional breakpoint written by hand

followUps:
Take memory snapshots and compare them. In Chrome DevTools open Memory, take a heap snapshot, do the suspect action several times, take a second snapshot and view the "Comparison". Objects whose count keeps growing are the leak.

Then use the Retainers panel to see what still points at them, often a global array, an unremoved event listener, a timer or a closure. Example: 1,000 clicks leave 1,000 detached DOM nodes held by a listener list. In Node, use --inspect and take the same snapshots, or watch process.memoryUsage().heapUsed climb after forced GC.

Pausing at a breakpoint freezes the whole event loop, so the process stops answering requests, health checks fail, and the load balancer or orchestrator may kill it. Open connections can also time out and retry, creating a flood when you resume.

Safer options: use logpoints (they log without stopping), reproduce in staging, take a heap or CPU profile (short pause), or attach to one instance that has been removed from the load balancer first.

A logpoint is a breakpoint that prints a message instead of pausing. In DevTools, right-click a line number, choose "Add logpoint" and type an expression such as 'user', user.id, total. Each time that line runs, the console shows the values.

It saves you from editing code to add console.log and from forgetting to remove it, and it works on code you cannot easily change, like a minified bundle with source maps. Nothing pauses, so it is also safe on timing-sensitive code.

code.title: Portable core with runtime adapters

followUps:
Use feature detection: test whether the thing you need exists, not which environment you think you are in. User-agent or runtime sniffing breaks when a new runtime copies the API, or when a browser spoofs its name.

const clone = typeof structuredClone === 'function'
  ? structuredClone(x)
  : JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x));

Sniffing is acceptable only for a known bug in one specific runtime, and then with a comment and a removal plan. Detect the capability, not the vendor.

Run the same test files against several runtimes through one command each, and let CI run them in parallel. Node has node --test; Deno and Bun run similar tests with deno test and bun test; for browsers use a headless Chromium through Playwright or Vitest browser mode.

Keep tests to the shared API and mock the adapters. Cloudflare's local workerd runtime (through Miniflare) covers the edge. Starting several lightweight runtimes in CI usually costs only a few minutes in total and catches an accidental Buffer import early.

code.title: Auditing install scripts of dependencies

followUps:
Slopsquatting is a supply-chain attack where an attacker publishes a malicious package under a name that an AI code assistant tends to invent ("hallucinate"). A developer or an automated agent then runs npm install on that made-up name and installs the attacker's code.

Defences: check that a package exists and has history before installing it, prefer packages already in your lockfile, use an allow-list or private registry for agents, and run installs with --ignore-scripts in a sandbox.

Node's permission model (--permission in Node 20+, stable in later releases) makes a process deny-by-default for risky actions, so you grant exactly what is needed.

node --permission --allow-fs-read=./data \
  --allow-fs-write=./out app.js

Without a grant, file reads, writes, child processes and worker threads throw ERR_ACCESS_DENIED. It limits damage from a compromised dependency, but it is not a full sandbox: native addons and bugs can still escape, so combine it with containers.

Provenance is a signed statement attached to a published package that says which source repository, commit and build workflow produced it. You publish it from a trusted CI with npm publish --provenance, and npm shows a verified badge.

Users can check that the tarball was really built from the public source and not uploaded from a stolen laptop or token. It does not prove the code is safe, only where it came from. Pair it with 2FA and trusted publishing so no long-lived token exists.

code.title: Live reference versus snapshot in logging

followUps:
Use the depth option. By default Node prints only 2 levels below the top and shows [Object] after that. Pass null for no limit.

console.dir(obj, { depth: null });
// or
console.log(require('util').inspect(obj,
  { depth: null, colors: true }));

The sample program shows { a: { b: { c: [Object] } } } by default and the full chain with depth: null. Printing a huge graph this way can flood the terminal, so a large depth like 5 is often enough.

console.table prints an array of objects (or an object of objects) as a table with one row per item and one column per key, which is easy to scan. console.trace prints a message plus the current call stack, so you can see who called this code.

console.table([{ id: 1, n: 'a' }, { id: 2, n: 'b' }]);
console.trace('how did we get here?');

Use table for lists of records and trace when a function runs from an unexpected place. In Node, trace writes to stderr.
